problem: The claim about divergence is inverted. A semiconductor laser's emitting facet is only a few micrometres across, and a small aperture gives large diffraction spread, so the beam diverges by roughly 10°–30° and is elliptical. The cavity acts on the longitudinal modes (narrow spectrum), not on the beam spread.
fix: The beam leaves the tiny facet as an elliptical cone that diverges by about 10°–30°, much more than a gas laser beam; the cavity mainly selects a narrow set of longitudinal modes, so the spectrum is narrow.

problem: 'More electrons sit in conduction-band states than in valence-band states at the same energy' is loose: conduction-band and valence-band states are separated by the band gap and do not lie at the same energy, so a student can misread the condition.
fix: Population inversion means the occupation probability at the conduction-band edge is larger than at the valence-band edge, i.e. the separation of the electron and hole quasi-Fermi levels exceeds the band gap energy (Efc − Efv > Eg).

where: Section 3, paragraph 'A GaAs laser at 873 nm is used...'
problem: 873 nm is the wavelength computed from the GaAs band gap; the named consumer products do not work at that wavelength. CD players use about 780 nm, barcode scanners usually 650–680 nm, so the sentence misleads on numbers.
fix: Near-infrared diode lasers of the GaAs family (roughly 780–850 nm) serve short-range links and optical mice; CD players use about 780 nm and barcode scanners about 650–680 nm. Which laser for which task is covered in 5.6.
